'''''Thunbergia grandiflora''''' is an evergreen [[liana|vine]] in the family [[Acanthaceae]].<ref name=weeds/> It is native to [[southeast Asia]], particularly [[Indochina]], and is widely naturalised elsewhere.<ref name=kew>{{cite web|title=Thunbergia grandiflora Roxb.|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:117460-3|website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref><ref name=GRIN/> Common names include '''Bengal clockvine''', '''Bengal trumpet''', '''blue skyflower''', '''blue thunbergia''', '''blue trumpetvine''', '''clockvine''', '''skyflower''' and '''skyvine'''.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=8 January 2013}}</ref> The specific epithet ''grandiflora'' means "large-flowered".<ref name=Missouri/>

==Description==
Plants may grow to about 20 metres in height and have a long root system with a deep [[tap root]], that can be as large as a small car.<ref name=weeds/> The stems are green, [[Pubescence (botany)|pubescent]] and quadrangular when young, becoming brown, rounded and woody with age.<ref>{{cite web |title=Blue thunbergia (*Thunbergia grandiflora*) |url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/blue-thunbergia |website=Brisbane City Council |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> 

The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and borne on [[Pedicel (botany)|stalks]] up to {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on}} long. They are bright green when young, becoming dark green with age and paler beneath, with a rough upper surface. The [[leaf blade]]s are highly variable in shape, ranging from [[Glossary of botanical terms|ovate]] and cordate to triangular or angularly lobed, and measure up to {{convert|22|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|15|cm|abbr=on}} wide, although they are typically smaller than those of the closely related ''[[Thunbergia laurifolia|T. laurifolia]]''.<ref name=weeds/> The leaves have an acute apex, prominently raised veins, with three to five primary veins arising from the base, and margins that may be entire, toothed or lobed.<ref name=wise>{{cite web |title=Laurel clock vine (*Thunbergia grandiflora*) |url=https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weed/Laurelclockvine |website=NSW WeedWise |publisher=NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> 

===Flowers===
The large, showy, trumpet-shaped flowers are borne in pendulous clusters and are up to {{convert|8|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|to|8|cm|abbr=on}} wide. The [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] has five rounded lobes, one longer than the others, and is typically pale blue, violet or mauve with a pale yellow to whitish throat and a white exterior. Flowers are borne on 4 to 5 cm long [[pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s and are subtended by a pair of leafy [[bract]]eoles, which are oblong to ovate, 15 to 40 mm long and 10 to 20 mm wide, with [[acuminate]] apices. The [[pubescence (botany)|pubescent]] [[sepal]]s are fused to form a greenish, ring-like [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] tube that is sometimes streaked with purple or red. Flowering may occur throughout the year but is most prolific during summer and autumn.<ref name=wise/><ref name=lucid/>

The fruit is a brown, oval [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] about {{convert|3|cm|abbr=on}} long with a long, pointed beak, containing two to four seeds.<ref name=weeds>{{cite web | url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/weeds-australia/profile/Thunbergia%20grandiflora | title=''Thunbergia grandiflora'' | publisher = Weeds Australia - Profiles | access-date=17 April 2021}}</ref> These are followed by pods containing seeds that are ejected several metres upon ripening. Plants also reproduce from segments that are washed down watercourses.<ref name=weeds/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Thunbergia grandiflora kz01.jpg|thumb|Flowers]]
With a minimum temperature of {{convert|10|-|13|C|F|abbr=on}}, this plant is cultivated as a houseplant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions,<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|page=1136}}</ref> and has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Thunbergia grandiflora''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/101497/Thunbergia-grandiflora/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 102 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 23 December 2018}}</ref> 

It is hardy in [[USDA hardiness zone]]s 10 and 11, where it grows best in fertile, organically rich, moist but well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade. In hotter climates, it benefits from light afternoon shade. In cooler regions, it is commonly cultivated as an [[annual plant|annual]] or overwintered indoors in containers. The species is propagated from [[seed]], [[cutting (plant)|cuttings]] or overwintered container-grown plants. The species readily regenerates from its expansive [[tuberous]] root system. Shoots arising from the tubers are easily separated and transplanted, making vegetative propagation simpler and more reliable than growing plants from seed or stem cuttings.<ref>{{cite web |title=Thunbergia |url=https://www.business.qld.gov.au/industries/farms-fishing-forestry/agriculture/biosecurity/plants/invasive/restricted/thunbergia |website=Business Queensland |publisher=Queensland Government |date=30 April 2026 |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> The species is generally free of serious insect [[Pest (organism)|pest]]s and diseases, although it may be susceptible to [[scale insect]]s, [[spider mite]]s and [[whitefly|whiteflies]].<ref name=Missouri>{{cite web |title=''Thunbergia grandiflora'' |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c941 |website=Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref>

==Distribution==
The plant is native to [[Assam]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Bhutan]], [[Cambodia]], South-Central China and Southeast China ([[Fujian Sheng]], [[Guangdong Sheng]], [[Guangxi Zhuangzu Zizhiqu]], [[Hainan Sheng]]), [[East Himalaya]],  [[Laos]], [[Peninsular Malaysia]], [[Myanmar]], [[Nepal]], [[Northeast India]], [[Thailand]] and [[Vietnam]].<ref name=kew/><ref name=GRIN/> 

It is widely naturalised in the coastal regions of [[Queensland]], where it is most common in the [[Electoral district of Cook|Cook pastoral district]]. Scattered populations also occur along the central and south-eastern Queensland coast. Outside Australia, the species has become naturalised in parts of [[South America]] ([[Guyana]], [[Ecuador]], [[Suriname]]), [[Singapore]], [[Central America]] (including [[Costa Rica]]), the southeastern [[United States]] (particularly [[Florida]]), the [[Mascarene Islands]] (including [[Réunion]], [[Mauritius]] and the [[Seychelles]]), and several [[Pacific Islands]], including [[Fiji]], [[Samoa]], [[Palau]] and [[Hawaii]]. It is an [[adventive plant]] in Mexico ([[Chiapas]]) and Guatemala.<ref name=GRIN/> 

===Weed status===
The species has become a serious [[invasive species|environmental weed]] in Australia on disturbed land along watercourses and in the wet tropics where it smothers other vegetation. It is commonly seen north of Sydney where it has been cultivated for many years.<ref name=weeds/> It thrives in tropical, subtropical and even warmer temperate regions, preferring frostless areas with productive, acidic, permeable soils. It is commonly established in [[riverbank|riverside]]s, in forests (particularly along its boundaries and [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed areas]]), in sparse timberlands, and along roadsides and fence lines.<ref name=wise/>

It develops an extensive [[tuber]]ous root system, with individual tubers weighing up to {{convert|70|kg|lb|abbr=on}}. The tubers readily resprout from numerous dormant buds following cutting or [[pruning]], making the species difficult to eradicate. The root system can damage [[riverbank]]s, [[footpath]]s, fences and building foundations. As a vigorous [[vine|climber]], the plant can smother vegetation up to {{convert|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} above ground, reducing light availability to the [[understorey]] and, in severe infestations, killing trees under the weight of its stems. Although it is not considered a major weed in parts of its native range, including [[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]] and [[Uganda]], it is a significant [[invasive species]] in [[Australia]], where it invades agricultural land and [[nature reserve]]s, forming dense infestations that can achieve complete [[groundcover]] and displace native vegetation.<ref name=lucid>{{cite web |title=Factsheet - ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' (Blue Thunbergia) |url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/eafrinet/weeds/key/weeds/Media/Html/Thunbergia_grandiflora_(Blue_Thunbergia).htm |website=Lucidcentral |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref>

==Ethnobotany and pharmacology==
In [[traditional medicine]], ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' has been used to treat a variety of ailments, including [[dysentery]], [[cataract]]s, [[diabetes]], [[gout]], [[hydrocele]], [[malaria]], [[rheumatism]], [[conjunctivitis]], [[elephantiasis]], stomach pain and [[bladder stone]]s. The leaves have been used to treat stomach ailments and as [[poultice]]s in India and [[Malaysia]]. In [[Assam]], India, the leaves are consumed as a [[leaf vegetable]] and are fed to [[domestic rabbit]]s. [[Phytochemical]] studies have reported that the leaves are rich in [[potassium]] salts, while the floral [[nectar]] contains high concentrations of [[sucrose]], together with [[glucose]] and [[fructose]].<ref>{{cite web |title=''Thunbergia grandiflora'' Roxb. |url=https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.upwta.1_96 |website=JSTOR Global Plants |publisher=ITHAKA |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> The plant is also used as a [[green manure]] and for poles, [[hedgerow|hedging]] and [[fuelwood]].<ref name=lucid/>

[[Phytochemical]] studies have identified numerous [[bioactive compound]]s in ''Thunbergia grandiflora'', including [[alkaloid]]s, [[flavonoid]]s, [[iridoid glycoside]]s, [[glycoside]]s, [[saponin]]s, [[tannin]]s and [[phenol|phenolic compounds]]. Identified constituents include [[quercetin]], [[kaempferol]] and [[limonene]]. Laboratory studies have reported [[antioxidant]], [[anti-inflammatory]], [[antimicrobial]], anti-[[arthritic]] and potential [[anticancer]] activity, although these findings are based primarily on experimental research and do not demonstrate clinical efficacy in humans.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aher |first1=Anilkumar |last2=Gawali |first2=Sonali |last3=Jadhav |first3=Pranjal |last4=Darade |first4=Chetan |last5=Kamble |first5=Vaishnavi |last6=Kharat |first6=Suraj |last7=Tamkhane |first7=Harshada |title=Pharmacognostic Review on ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' Roxb. (Family – Acanthaceae) |journal=Research Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=135–142 |year=2025 |doi=10.52711/0975-4385.2025.00023 |url=https://rjpponline.org/AbstractView.aspx?PID=2025-17-2-10 |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> However, these [[pharmacological]] findings are based primarily on experimental studies and do not constitute evidence of clinical efficacy in humans. The study found that a methanolic leaf extract of the plant exhibited anti-[[trypanosomiasis|trypanosomal]] activity under experimental conditions. Phytochemical analysis identified several secondary metabolites, including [[diphyllin]] and avacennone B, which computational modelling suggested may interact with [[enzymes]] involved in the [[parasite]]'s metabolism. The authors concluded that the species warrants further investigation as a potential source of bioactive compounds for the treatment of [[trypanosomiasis]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=El-Nashar |first1=Heba A. S. |last2=Sayed |first2=Ahmed M. |last3=El-Sherief |first3=Hany A. M. |last4=Rateb |first4=Mostafa E. |last5=Akil |first5=Lina |last6=Khadra |first6=Ibrahim |last7=Majrashi |first7=Taghreed A. |last8=Al-Rashood |first8=Sara T. |last9=Binjubair |first9=Faizah A. |last10=El Hassab |first10=Mahmoud A. |last11=Eldehna |first11=Wagdy M. |last12=Abdelmohsen |first12=Usama Ramadan |last13=Mostafa |first13=Nada M. |title=Metabolomic profile, anti-trypanosomal potential and molecular docking studies of ''Thunbergia grandifolia'' |journal=Journal of Enzyme Inhibition and Medicinal Chemistry |volume=38 |issue=1 |year=2023 |article-number=2199950 |doi=10.1080/14756366.2023.2199950 |pmc=10120545 |pmid=37026661}}</ref>

Laboratory studies have reported that ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' exhibits [[antibacterial]] activity. In one study, extracts of T. grandiflora and ''[[Thunbergia fragrans]]'' produced greater inhibition of ''[[Staphylococcus aureus]]'' growth than the [[streptomycin]] control under the experimental conditions tested.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sultana |first1=Khairun |last2=Chatterjee |first2=Soumya |last3=Roy |first3=Ananya |last4=Chandra |first4=Indrani |title=Evaluation of phytochemical and antibacterial activity of selected species of ''Thunbergia'' |journal=Asian Journal of Green Chemistry |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=59–74 |year=2019 |doi=10.22034/AJGC.2019.66293 |url=https://www.ajgreenchem.com/article_218530.html |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref> A laboratory study investigated the [[antioxidant]] and [[acetylcholinesterase inhibitor|anticholinesterase]] properties of ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' in relation to [[Alzheimer's disease]]. The extracts demonstrated antioxidant activity and inhibition of [[cholinesterase]] enzymes under experimental conditions. The authors suggested that further studies, including dose-response investigations, are needed to evaluate the species' potential as a source of compounds for Alzheimer's disease research.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Uddin |first1=Md. Josim |last2=Alam |first2=Mohammad Nazmul |last3=Biswas |first3=Kushal |last4=Rahman |first4=Md. Atiar |title=In vitro antioxidative and cholinesterase inhibitory properties of ''Thunbergia grandiflora'' leaf extract |journal=Cogent Food & Agriculture |volume=2 |issue=1 |year=2016 |article-number=1256929 |doi=10.1080/23311932.2016.1256929 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/23311932.2016.1256929 |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref>
